title: Balod district overview
text: Balod is a district in Chhattisgarh with its headquarters in Balod town. The official district portal states that Balod became a district on 1 January 2012, having previously been part of Durg district. The portal gives the district area as 352,700 hectares (3,527 km²). Balod town lies near the Tandula River and has an average elevation of about 324 metres. The portal's stated coordinates for the town are approximately 20.73° N and 81.2° E; a separate Hindi homepage transcription appears to show a different longitude, so coordinates should be verified before geospatial use.
quality_flag: Town coordinate discrepancy in portal text; distinguish district area from town location

title: Balod district formation history
text: The official district history page says Balod was among the districts formed in 2012 and became the 27th district of Chhattisgarh. It was notified as a civil district on 1 January 2012, while the revenue district was declared from 10 January 2012. Before district formation, the area was part of Durg district.
quality_flag: Official historical summary; limited historical detail beyond district formation

These are historical Census 2011 figures and must not be presented as current population estimates.

title: Balod geography and climate
text: The district geography page describes Balod as having a tropical wet-and-dry or savanna climate, with an average elevation of about 324 metres at the district headquarters. The portal reports average annual rainfall of 1,089.8 mm and says about 93% of annual rainfall occurs between June and September, with rainfall generally lower toward the north-east and south-west of the district. These are portal-level climatological figures; the reference period for the average is not specified.

Tandula, Kharkhara and Gondli dams are described as major irrigation sources for the district. Specific current reservoir storage, irrigated acreage and dam operating status are not provided in the short district profile.

The portal's claim that minerals contribute about 78% of revenue lacks a clear accounting period or methodology in the short overview and should be treated as an unverified portal claim rather than a current audited statistic.

title: District overview and formation
text: Balrampur-Ramanujganj district lies in northern Chhattisgarh and was carved out of the erstwhile Surguja district, coming into existence on 17 January 2012. It borders Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Madhya Pradesh. The district is hilly and forested, with parts of the Satpuda hill ranges, and its headquarters is Balrampur.

title: History of Bastar District
text: The official Bastar district history page states that Jagdalpur is the headquarters of Bastar district and Bastar division. It describes the region as historically associated with Dakshin Kaushal and says the Bastar princely state was established around 1324 CE by Anaam Dev, who left Warangal and established a kingdom in Bastar. The page names rulers including Hamir Dev, Baital Dev, Purushottam Dev, Pratap Dev, Dikpal Dev and Rajpal Dev. It says the initial capital was Bastar town and was later moved to Jagdalpur. Maharaja Praveer Chandra Bhanj Dev is described as the last ruler, with the period 1936–1948, and the princely state is said to have merged with India in 1948. The page also notes that Kanker and Dantewada were carved out in 1999, and lists Bastar Mahal, Bastar Dussehra, Dalpat Sagar, Chitrakote and Tirathgarh waterfalls, and Kutumsar and Kailash caves as tourist attractions. The page reports Census 2011 population of 834,375 (413,706 men and 420,669 women) and mentions Gond, Maria, Muria, Bhatra, Halba and Dhruva communities. Historical and population details are reported as stated by the district website; population and administrative figures should be interpreted with their reference dates.

title: बस्तर जिले का इतिहास
text: बस्तर जिला प्रशासन की आधिकारिक हिंदी वेबसाइट के अनुसार, बस्तर जिले और बस्तर संभाग का मुख्यालय जगदलपुर है। वेबसाइट क्षेत्र को ऐतिहासिक रूप से दक्षिण कौशल से जोड़ती है और बताती है कि लगभग 1324 ईस्वी में अन्नम देव ने वारंगल छोड़कर बस्तर में रियासत स्थापित की। वेबसाइट में हमीर देव, बैताल देव, पुरुषोत्तम देव, प्रताप देव, दिकपाल देव और राजपाल देव जैसे शासकों का उल्लेख है। प्रारंभिक राजधानी बस्तर में थी, जिसे बाद में जगदलपुर स्थानांतरित किया गया। वेबसाइट महाराजा प्रवीर चन्द्र भंज देव को अंतिम शासक बताती है और रियासत का भारत में विलय 1948 में बताती है। पृष्ठ में 1999 में कांकेर और दंतेवाड़ा को अलग जिले बनाए जाने का भी उल्लेख है। बस्तर महल, बस्तर दशहरा, दलपत सागर, चित्रकोट और तीरथगढ़ जलप्रपात तथा कुटुमसर और कैलाश गुफाओं को पर्यटन स्थलों में गिना गया है। वेबसाइट 2011 की जनगणना के अनुसार जनसंख्या 8,34,375 बताती है। इन ऐतिहासिक और जनसांख्यिकीय विवरणों को वेबसाइट-आधारित जानकारी के रूप में रखें और आंकड़ों के संदर्भ वर्ष को सुरक्षित रखें।
category: जिला इतिहास; रियासत; जनजातीय संस्कृति; पर्यटन

text: बस्तर जिला प्रशासन की आधिकारिक हिंदी वेबसाइट के अनुसार, जिला छत्तीसगढ़ के बस्तर संभाग के अंतर्गत आता है। जिला कलेक्टर एवं दंडाधिकारी जिले के प्रशासक होते हैं और कानून-व्यवस्था बनाए रखने, नियमों के पालन तथा सरकारी योजनाओं के क्रियान्वयन के लिए जिम्मेदार होते हैं। यह पृष्ठ प्रशासनिक भूमिका का वर्णन करता है; इसे सभी प्रशासनिक इकाइयों की संपूर्ण सूची नहीं माना जाना चाहिए।

text: बस्तर जिला प्रशासन की आधिकारिक हिंदी वेबसाइट पर चार उपखंड दिए गए हैं: जगदलपुर, बस्तर, लोहंडीगुडा और तोकापाल। सात विकासखंडों के नाम हैं: जगदलपुर, बस्तर, बकावंड, लोहंडीगुडा, तोकापाल, बास्तानार और दरभा। वेबसाइट पर संबंधित कार्यालयों के पते और पदनाम दिए गए हैं। प्रशासनिक सूचियां बदल सकती हैं, इसलिए वर्तमान जानकारी के लिए नवीनतम जिला अधिसूचना से पुष्टि करें।

title: Economy of Bastar District
text: The official Bastar district economy page identifies agriculture and collection of forest produce as major foundations of the district economy. Paddy is described as the main crop, especially during the kharif season. Other crops mentioned include urad, arhar, jowar, maize, sesame, linseed, mustard, gram, wheat and kodo-kutki. The page says that collecting and selling forest produce supplements agricultural income. Items listed include tendu leaves, lac, tamarind, amchur and other forest products. Animal husbandry, poultry and fisheries also support livelihoods. The page discusses low irrigation and fertilizer use and suggests rainwater harvesting as a possibility. Some wording on the page appears to be machine-translated or unclear, so exact technical figures should be verified before reuse.
category: Local economy; agriculture; forest produce; livelihoods

title: बस्तर जिले की अर्थव्यवस्था
text: बस्तर जिला प्रशासन की आधिकारिक वेबसाइट के अनुसार, जिले की अर्थव्यवस्था का प्रमुख आधार कृषि और वनोपज का संग्रहण है। खरीफ मौसम में धान मुख्य फसल है। वेबसाइट में उड़द, अरहर, ज्वार, मक्का, तिल, अलसी, सरसों, चना, गेहूं और कोदो-कुटकी जैसी अन्य फसलों का भी उल्लेख है। वनोपज का संग्रह और बिक्री कृषि से होने वाली आय को सहारा देते हैं। वेबसाइट में तेंदूपत्ता, लाख, इमली, आमचूर और अन्य वन उत्पादों का उल्लेख है। पशुपालन, मुर्गीपालन और मत्स्य पालन भी आजीविका में योगदान देते हैं। पृष्ठ सिंचाई और उर्वरक के कम उपयोग पर चर्चा करता है तथा वर्षा जल संचयन की संभावना बताता है। पृष्ठ की कुछ भाषा अस्पष्ट या मशीन-अनुवाद जैसी है, इसलिए सटीक तकनीकी आंकड़ों को उपयोग से पहले सत्यापित करें।
language: Hindi (translated summary; source page in English)

title: Bastar District Survey Report 2026 — overview and geography
text: The District Survey Report (DSR) for Bastar district was compiled by the Regional Office of the Directorate of Geology and Mining, Jagdalpur, using information provided by different departments through the District Mining Officer, Bastar. The report cover identifies it as a 2026 report for sand mining or riverbed mining. Its introduction places Bastar in southeastern Chhattisgarh and identifies Jagdalpur as district headquarters. The report lists seven blocks: Jagdalpur, Bastar, Bakawand, Darbha, Tokapal, Bastanar and Lohandiguda. It cites Census 2011 population of 834,375 (413,706 males and 420,669 females) and says more than 70% of the population belongs to indigenous tribal communities. The report gives geographical area as 6,596.90 km². These demographic figures are historical 2011 Census data, not current estimates.

For minor minerals and riverbed materials, it describes sand and clay as construction inputs and says two sand blocks have been leased along the Bhaskali River near Bajawand village. These counts and locations reflect the report's stated snapshot and should be checked against later mining department updates.

title: Bastar culture and heritage — overview
text: The official Bastar district Culture & Heritage page describes Bastar as a place with longstanding cultural traditions associated with forest-dwelling and tribal communities. It highlights Bastar Dussehra, memorial pillars, and the Ghotul tradition. The page was last updated on 25 September 2018, so descriptions should be treated as the district website's published account rather than a comprehensive or recently verified ethnographic source.

title: Bastar Dussehra — festival traditions
text: According to the official Bastar district Culture & Heritage page, Bastar Dussehra is distinctive because it is described as lasting around 75 days and does not include the burning of a Ravana effigy. The page says the festival begins with a ritual in which the first wood for a chariot is brought from the forest; this is called Pat Jatra. It concludes with Muria Durbar, described by the page as a gathering where the Maharaja's court listens to public concerns. This is the website's account, last updated 25 September 2018; dates and current festival arrangements should be checked with current official event notices.
category: Bastar Dussehra; festival; Pat Jatra; Muria Durbar

title: Bastar memorial pillars — Gudi tradition
text: The official Bastar district Culture & Heritage page describes a memorial custom known as a deceased or memorial pillar, particularly among Maria and Muria communities in southern Bastar. It says these pillars are called 'Gudi' in the local language and describes stone markers placed at ancestral burial locations. The source is a short district-webpage description last updated in 2018; terminology and community-specific details should be corroborated with local cultural experts or authoritative ethnographic sources before making broad claims.
category: tribal heritage; memorial pillars; Maria; Muria; Gudi

title: Ghotul tradition in Bastar
text: The official Bastar district Culture & Heritage page says the Ghotul tradition is associated with Madia communities in Bastar. It describes a village-edge mud structure used as a gathering place during festivals and notes that some structures have open floors or lack walls. The source's description is brief and dates to 2018. Avoid generalizing this account to all tribal communities or treating it as a full description of present-day practice.
category: Ghotul; community traditions; Madia; cultural heritage

title: Traditional handicrafts of Bastar
text: The official Bastar district Handicraft (Art and Culture) page groups traditional Bastar crafts into woodwork, bamboo art, soil/clay art, and metal arts. Examples described include wooden figures and decorations; bamboo chairs, baskets, mats and household items; clay figures, pots and decorative utensils; and metal objects such as deities, ritual figures and home furnishings. The page says these crafts use conventional tools and often reflect the rural life and cultural practices of local communities. Last updated 25 September 2018.
category: handicrafts; woodwork; bamboo; clay; metal craft

title: Dhokra and bell-metal craft in Bastar
text: The official Bastar district Handicraft page highlights Dhokra handicraft and bell-metal craft. It describes Dhokra materials as including cow dung, paddy husk, red soil and beeswax, with wax wires used for contours and decoration. It also notes that metal craft is used to make figures associated with worship, tribal culture and home decoration. This summary reflects the district website's description, last updated in 2018; specific technical details should be corroborated with craft practitioners or specialist sources.

title: Places of interest in Bastar — overview
text: The official Bastar district Places of Interest page describes the district as a destination known for forests, tribal culture, natural resources and handicrafts. It identifies Jagdalpur as the district headquarters and lists the Indravati River, Anthropological Museum at Dharampura, Bastar Palace, Bastar Dussehra, Dalpat Sagar, Chitrakote Waterfall, Tirathgarh Waterfall, Kotumsar Cave and Kailash Cave among notable attractions. The page gives the district area as 6,596.90 square kilometres. Tourism descriptions and distances on the page should be checked against current official guidance before travel.
category: tourism; geography; culture; heritage; natural attractions

title: Chitrakote Waterfall — Bastar
text: Chitrakote Waterfall is located on the Indravati River in Bastar district. The official district page gives its height as approximately 90 feet and its distance as about 40 km from Jagdalpur and 273 km from Raipur. It describes the waterfall as horseshoe-shaped and notes that its appearance changes with the season and water flow. The page recommends July to October for a dramatic monsoon view, but visitors should check local weather, access and safety notices before visiting.

title: Tirathgarh Waterfall — Kanger Valley
text: Tirathgarh Waterfall is within the Kanger Valley area of Bastar district. The official page places it about 35 km from Jagdalpur and describes water cascading down a height of around 300 feet. It is associated with the Kanger Valley landscape and is listed as a major natural attraction. The source gives October to April as a suitable period while also mentioning the rainy season; actual access and conditions vary with rainfall and official park rules.
category: tourism; waterfall; Kanger Valley National Park; nature

title: Kanger Valley National Park — Bastar
text: Kanger Valley National Park is described by the official Bastar district page as being about 34 km from Jagdalpur and having been declared a national park in 1982. The page highlights its mixed deciduous forests, including sal, teak and bamboo, as well as wildlife and bird diversity. Attractions associated with the park include Kotumsar, Kailash and Dandak caves and Tirathgarh Waterfall. Access to caves and park areas may be seasonal or regulated, so current visitor guidance should be checked.
category: tourism; national park; biodiversity; forests; wildlife

title: Kotumsar Cave — Bastar
text: Kotumsar Cave is a limestone cave in the Kanger Valley area near Jagdalpur. The official district page describes its underground formations and reports that the cave was studied after its discovery in 1951 by geographer Dr. Shankar Tiwari. The page includes geological and prehistoric-human claims that should not be treated as scientifically verified without consulting specialist sources. Cave access may be restricted during the monsoon or when conditions are unsafe.

title: Kailash Cave — Bastar
text: Kailash Cave is one of the limestone caves in Kanger Valley National Park. The official Bastar district tourist page says it was discovered on 22 March 1993 and describes stalactite and stalagmite formations resembling a Shivlinga. It reports a known length of about 1,000 feet and depth of about 120 feet. The page says the cave typically reopens from 16 October to 15 June and closes during the monsoon; visitors should confirm current dates and access arrangements with park authorities.
category: tourism; cave; limestone formations; natural heritage

title: Cultural and heritage attractions in Bastar
text: The official Bastar district page lists Bastar Palace, Bastar Dussehra, Dalpat Sagar and the Anthropological Museum at Dharampura among cultural attractions. These figures are page-specific estimates, not live navigation distances; verify route and road conditions before travel.

title: Sukma Accommodation Directory — Official Portal Snapshot
text: The official Sukma accommodation page lists lodging options in the town, including Circuit House, Hotel Raj Palace and Shree Shree Hotel. This is a directory listing, not a verified real-time inventory. The page does not establish current availability, rates, amenities, accessibility or reservation status. Confirm details directly with the property or district administration before relying on the listing for travel planning.

title: Sukma Government Departments — Official Directory
text: The official Sukma departments page says it provides details such as addresses, contact information and schemes for selected government departments. Departments linked from the page include Health, Education, Animal Husbandry and Khadya (Food/Civil Supplies); the official site map additionally lists Revenue, Panchayat, Tribal Welfare, Mining, Agriculture, Women and Child Development, and Election. Treat this as a directory index. For current scheme eligibility, contact details or service procedures, use the relevant department's current page rather than relying on an index summary.

title: Sukma Food and Civil Supplies — Department Functions
text: The official Sukma Khadya (Food/Civil Supplies) page describes the department's functions as public distribution of essential commodities through fair-price shops, Aadhaar-based e-PoS distribution under applicable rules, food-grain procurement under Minimum Support Price, supply to government schools and welfare hostels, nutrition support to Anganwadi centres, and facilitation of eligible Ujjwala connections. The page also displays ration-card counts, but those counts are a dated snapshot with unclear reference date and should not be treated as current beneficiary totals without verification. Personal contact details are deliberately excluded from this general RAG record.

title: Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17 — Official Document Metadata
text: The official Sukma statistical-report listing identifies a document titled “District Statistical report 2016-17,” listed on 26 December 2018 with a displayed file size of 333 KB. This record contains document metadata only; the PDF's tables and text have not been extracted into this record. If used for RAG, retrieve the original document, capture page numbers and reference periods, and mark its figures as historical rather than current.

title: Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17: Administrative and geographic profile
text: Historical source: Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17, published/listed by the district portal on 26 December 2018. The report’s district summary table gives a geographical area of 5,635.79 square kilometres, 385 villages (371 inhabited), 135 gram panchayats, 3 Janpad Panchayats, 1 Nagar Palika and 2 Nagar Panchayats. Its tehsil table gives area figures of Konta 3,820.59 km², Chhindgarh 848.71 km² and Sukma 966.49 km². These are historical figures from the 2016–17 report and conflict with the current district homepage’s area figure of 5,897.79 km²; retain both values with their source dates rather than treating either as current truth. PDF text extraction is OCR-derived and the original table should be checked before high-stakes use.

title: Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17: Census 2011 population indicators
text: The district’s Statistical Report 2016–17 includes a Census 2011 demographic table. Its extracted table reports district population of 250,159, with 124,048 males and 126,111 females; sex ratio 1,017 females per 1,000 males; decadal population growth 8.16%; and literacy 34.81%. It also gives tehsil-level population figures: Konta 105,596, Sukma 64,891 and Chhindgarh 79,672. These numbers differ from other official Sukma pages/reports that give different Census 2011 totals and literacy values. Treat this as a source-specific historical report figure, not a reconciled definitive statistic. OCR extraction and possible administrative-boundary/table interpretation need manual verification.

title: Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17: Historical rainfall observations
text: The rainfall table in Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17 gives annual rainfall by tehsil for selected years. For 2016–17, it reports Konta 1,189.4 mm, Sukma 1,517.2 mm and Chhindgarh 1,502.2 mm. The report also contains earlier-year entries, but availability differs by tehsil/year. These are historical observations for the stated year and should not be used as current climate normals or forecasts. The PDF text layer is OCR-derived; validate the table image before using these figures in calculations.

title: Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17: Education and health infrastructure
text: The historical report includes block-level tables for education and health infrastructure. Its education table lists 725 primary schools, 212 middle schools, 19 high schools and 12 higher-secondary schools across the three development blocks, with additional institution categories shown separately. Its health table lists 3 Community Health Centres, 13 Primary Health Centres and 81 sub-health centres across the district. These are figures reported for the 2016–17 statistical publication, not current service availability. Because the source is a scanned/legacy Hindi PDF with OCR extraction, category alignment and totals should be checked against the original tables before operational use.

title: Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17: Land use, forests and agriculture tables
text: The 2016–17 report contains sections on land use, agricultural holdings, crop area and production, irrigation, livestock and poultry, fisheries, forest area and forest produce, and mineral production. Its contents identify crop-area tables by major crop and season, irrigation sources and irrigated area, livestock/poultry counts, and forest-circle area. The report’s administrative summary gives total area as 333,530 hectares, including 107,909 hectares of occupied area and 225,621 hectares of unoccupied area, but the table terminology and figures require review against the PDF image. Use this record as a topic-level guide to historical tables; detailed crop/mineral values should be extracted and manually verified before being added to the RAG knowledge base.

title: Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17: Subject coverage and extraction status
text: The official 107-page Sukma District Statistical Report 2016–17 is a broad statistical compendium. Its table of contents covers geographic and administrative structure; population, literacy and working population; agriculture and allied services; forest statistics; mining and quarrying; industry and employment; electricity; education; health and public health; drinking water and roads; public distribution; banking; transport and communications; crime and justice; local bodies; revenue and finance; newspapers and vital registration. The current RAG collection has extracted a small set of topic summaries and selected figures from the PDF text layer. It has not yet exhaustively extracted all 107 pages or manually verified all tables, so this is a source inventory rather than a claim of complete report coverage.

title: A brief introduction to District Sukma (2017): historical administrative profile
text: The district portal lists a document titled “A brief introduction to District Sukma,” dated 12 July 2017, with a PDF size of approximately 530 KB. The linked PDF is a short historical district profile covering administrative units, population and local institutions, education and health facilities, forest circles, irrigation projects, markets, revenue villages, land area and tourist sites. Some figures in the legacy document differ from current portal pages and the later 2016–17 statistical report. Preserve it as a dated historical source and do not merge its numbers with current values without checking reference year and administrative boundaries. The PDF text extraction is legacy Hindi OCR and needs manual review for individual figures.

title: Sukma Potential Linked Credit Plan 2016–17: Agro-climatic profile and rainfall
text: A NABARD Potential Linked Credit Plan (PLP) 2016–17 district profile describes Sukma as part of Zone VIII — Eastern Plateau and Hills (Bastar Plateau Region), with predominantly red sandy loam and red soils. It reports a total geographical area of 5,635.79 km² and normal rainfall of 1,690 mm. Actual rainfall shown for 2012–13, 2013–14 and 2014–15 is 2,068 mm, 1,758 mm and 1,466 mm respectively. These are historical planning-profile values, not current rainfall or climate normals validated for present use.

title: Sukma Potential Linked Credit Plan 2016–17: Land use and cropping
text: The NABARD PLP 2016–17 district profile lists total reported area as 563,579 hectares. It gives forest land as 210,814 ha; area not available for cultivation 22,702 ha; permanent pasture and grazing land 26,811 ha; cultivable wasteland 47,355 ha; current fallow 6,542 ha; other fallow 17,671 ha; net sown area 96,348 ha; gross cropped area 97,389 ha; and area cultivated more than once 1,041 ha. The reported cropping intensity is 105%. These are historical figures copied from the plan profile; category totals and the underlying source year should be checked before using them as current land-use statistics.

title: Sukma Potential Linked Credit Plan 2016–17: Distribution of agricultural landholdings
text: The NABARD PLP 2016–17 profile reports 32,327 agricultural holdings in Sukma. It classifies 6,245 holdings (19%) as up to 1 hectare, 12,974 holdings (40%) as more than 1 and up to 2 hectares, and 13,108 holdings (41%) as above 2 hectares. The report’s table gives corresponding area shares as 10%, 13% and 77%. These are historical profile values and the area/holding classification should be validated against the original table before use in quantitative analysis.

title: Sukma Potential Linked Credit Plan 2016–17: Worker profile
text: The NABARD PLP 2016–17 district profile gives an approximate worker profile, in thousands: 32 cultivators, of whom 19 are small/marginal farmers; 10 agricultural labourers; 4 workers in household industries; 4 workers engaged in allied agro-activities; and 45 other workers. The source presents these as rounded figures in a district planning profile, not a current labour-force estimate. Do not combine these rounded figures with later employment data without preserving the reference year and definitions.

title: Sukma Potential Linked Credit Plan 2016–17: Demographic profile
text: The NABARD PLP 2016–17 profile presents rounded demographic indicators for Sukma, in thousands: population 250, male population 124, female population 126, rural population 223 and urban population 17. It reports Scheduled Caste population of 11 thousand, Scheduled Tribe population of 174 thousand, and literate population of 91 thousand (62 thousand male and 29 thousand female). These are rounded historical profile values, likely based on Census-era statistics; use exact Census tables for precise calculations and retain this source as a dated secondary planning summary.

title: Sukma Potential Linked Credit Plan 2016–17: Village and health infrastructure
text: The NABARD PLP 2016–17 district profile lists 379 inhabited villages and 132 panchayats. It reports 259 villages electrified, 39 villages with post offices, 858 Anganwadis, 12 Primary Health Centres, 81 Primary Health Sub-Centres and 3 hospitals. These figures differ from some other official district pages and later administrative listings. Treat them as historical planning-profile figures, preserve their source and year, and verify definitions and coverage before using them to answer present-day service-availability questions.

title: Sukma Health Department: Health facility counts by block
text: The official Sukma Health page lists 3 Community Health Centres, 15 Primary Health Centres and 95 Sub Health Centres across the district. Its block table gives Sukma: 0 CHCs, 3 PHCs, 21 sub-health centres; Chindgarh: 1 CHC, 6 PHCs, 39 sub-health centres; Konta: 2 CHCs, 6 PHCs, 35 sub-health centres. The same page says District Hospital Sukma began operating at Kumharras in 2016 as a 100-bed hospital and that the Mother and Child Health building was inaugurated in November 2019. These are page-reported infrastructure details; current operational status and bed availability are not independently verified. This count differs from older statistical sources and should be retained with the source and collection date.

title: Sukma Agriculture Department: Official department page inventory
text: The official district portal provides a dedicated Agriculture department page. This record preserves the page as an authoritative starting point for agriculture-related district information, but the page content available during this collection pass did not expose enough substantive text to create a reliable summary of current schemes, crop production, input distribution or farmer services. Use the linked page for further extraction and do not treat this metadata record itself as evidence of particular schemes or current agricultural statistics.

title: Sukma land survey and resurvey status: Government of India DILRMP dashboard
text: The Department of Land Resources' DILRMP survey/resurvey dashboard reports a total mapped area of 1,895.51 km² for Sukma in its displayed survey-status table, with 1,850.88 km² surveyed (97.65%), 30.98 km² rural area and 13.65 km² urban area; it lists 282 villages in the survey-status table. These fields describe the programme's survey coverage and are not equivalent to the district's full geographical area or total village count. The dashboard includes tehsil entries such as Chhindgarh, Dornapal, Gadiras, Jagargunda, Konta, Sukma and Tongpal. Capture the dashboard date and definitions before using these numbers; do not confuse survey coverage with district area.

title: Sukma watershed baseline survey: Land classification and cropped area
text: The Government of India's WDC-PMKSY baseline survey dashboard displays two Sukma watershed projects, SUKMA-WDC-1/2021-22 and SUKMA-WDC-2/2021-22. Combined project area is shown as 13,166 hectares, plot area as 14,267.24 hectares, net sown area as 739.57 hectares, gross cropped area as 749.81 hectares, and total value of output as ₹295.36 lakh. The dashboard's land classification columns include cultivable wasteland, degraded land, rainfed, forest land and others. These values apply to the listed watershed project areas, not to the whole district; the report itself warns that total income is the total value of output.

title: Sukma Bank BC List: Official district document inventory
text: The Sukma district Documents page lists a document titled “Sukma Bank BC List,” dated 20 May 2022, with a listed size of 403 KB. This record captures document metadata only. The file contents have not been extracted in this pass, so no names, banking correspondents, contact details, service locations or current operating status should be inferred from this record. If extracted later, treat it as a dated directory and avoid presenting it as a current list without validation.

title: Sukma District Survey Report 2025: Official document metadata
text: The official Sukma portal lists a District Survey Report dated 27 November 2025, available as a 4 MB PDF. A separate 2026 District Survey Report is also listed on the portal, dated 15 October 2026. This record captures the 2025 report's title/date/availability as source metadata; it does not represent a full extraction of the 2025 PDF. For questions about sand mining, geology, river beds or environmental clearances, extract and validate the report's actual content and distinguish it from the 2026 report.

title: Sukma District Survey Report 2025: Geographic and administrative profile
text: The Sukma District Survey Report 2025 was prepared by the Directorate of Geology and Mining, Chhattisgarh, Regional Office Jagdalpur, and updated under instructions dated 15 September 2025. The PDF is 39 pages. Its general profile reports district area 5,897.79 km², coordinates 17°46′55″–18°46′26″ N and 80°55′20″–81°57′30″ E, seven tehsils (Sukma, Konta, Chhindgarh, Gadiras, Jagargunda, Tongpal and Dornapal), 146 panchayats and 393 villages, Census 2011 population 270,821, density 45 persons/km², and forest area 290,652.713 hectares. The report's 393-village and 146-panchayat figures differ from other district portal pages; preserve the report-specific values and verify administrative definitions before resolving conflicts.

title: Sukma District Survey Report 2025: Geology and mineral resources
text: The 2025 District Survey Report describes rock units including the Eastern Ghat Supergroup, Bengpal Group, Dongargarh granite, Abujhmar Group and Sabri Group, with lithologies such as granulite, charnockite, gneiss, schist, amphibolite, quartzite, granite, sandstone, limestone, shale and alluvium. It identifies reported economic mineral occurrences primarily as tin in the Kikirpal area and corundum in the Nagaras area. It also mentions building materials such as aggregate, sand, murum, ordinary stone and brick clay. These are report-referenced geological occurrences and do not imply that every material is currently being mined or commercially available.

title: Sukma District Survey Report 2025: Mining leases and royalty figures
text: The report's general profile lists one major-mineral mining lease covering 11.541 hectares, two minor-mineral quarry leases covering 5.389 hectares, and nine notified sand leases covering 34.513 hectares. It reports major-mineral royalty/revenue of ₹102,173 for 2020–25 and minor-mineral revenue of ₹23,213,078 for the same period in the profile table. Other royalty tables in the PDF show year-by-year values and some OCR/table-layout inconsistencies, so the aggregate figures should be treated as report-specific and cross-checked against the original table before numerical analysis. Lease counts and areas are as stated in the 2025 report, not a live lease register.

title: Sukma District Survey Report 2025: Sand production and royalty, FY 2020–21 to 2024–25
text: The sand production table in the 2025 District Survey Report gives annual production and royalty as follows: FY 2020–21, 51,200 m³ and ₹2,560,000; FY 2021–22, 26,492 m³ and ₹1,324,600; FY 2022–23, 7,412 m³ and ₹370,600; FY 2023–24, 391 m³ and ₹19,550; FY 2024–25, 0 m³ and ₹0. The report totals 85,495 m³ and ₹4,274,750 across these five years. These values are directly represented in the PDF text layer, but validate the original table image before production use. They are historical report figures, not a statement about current sand availability or legal extraction status.

title: Sukma District Survey Report 2025: Forest cover, agriculture and irrigation
text: The 2025 report describes approximately 65% of Sukma district as forest-covered, with Sal and Sagaun named as principal tree types. It characterizes agriculture as predominantly rain-fed and paddy as the principal crop. Other crops mentioned include kodo-kutki, maize, pigeon pea, sorghum, chickpea, peanuts and vegetables; fruit crops mentioned include mango, guava, papaya, cashew, lemon and banana. The report states that only about 1% of net sown area has irrigation facilities and mentions initiatives promoting millet, organic and natural farming, micro-irrigation and mechanization. These are statements in the district survey report; program implementation and current crop statistics are not independently verified here.

title: Sukma District Survey Report 2025: River system and sand replenishment study
text: The report identifies the Sabari/Sabri as a principal river flowing through the district and names the Phool Nadi and Malenjar/Malanger among other rivers or streams. It places Sukma in the Indravati Basin and states that a sand replenishment study had not been conducted for the Sabari River and its tributaries, noting the need for such a study. The report includes sections on river drainage, sediment deposition, rainfall, groundwater levels and geohydrology, but much of the rainfall and water-level information is presented in maps or scanned tables that were not numerically transcribed in this record. Do not infer current water levels or sand replenishment rates from this summary.

title: Animal Husbandry and Livestock Statistics in Sukma
text: The official Sukma district Animal Husbandry page provides livestock and poultry counts, but the page was last updated on 22 December 2018, so the figures must be treated as historical and not as current livestock estimates. It lists cattle as 268,013; buffaloes 41,738; goats 106,626; sheep 5,403; swine 55,423; and other animals 39, with a stated total livestock count of 477,242 and total poultry of 289,244. The page lists six veterinary hospitals, 13 veterinary dispensaries, and one mobile hospital unit for the district. The category values and totals should be checked against the underlying livestock census because the source uses the label “Catal” for cattle and does not clearly state the enumeration year.

title: School Inventory and Education Challenges in Sukma
text: The official Sukma district Education page describes challenges including disparities in school quality and shortages of specialist teachers in higher grades, including mathematics, physics, chemistry and English. It discusses residential Ashram Shalas for children from remote villages and POTA Cabin Ashrams for students who have dropped out. Its school-at-a-glance table lists 1,054 schools across three blocks: Chhindgarh 405, Konta 375 and Sukma 274. The table reports 61 clusters in total. These figures are a snapshot from the district portal, whose displayed page was last updated on 29 September 2026; they should not be assumed to be a live school count. The abbreviated school-type columns are retained on the source page and need careful interpretation before using individual category totals.

title: आदिवासी कल्याण: छात्रावास, आश्रम और छात्रवृत्ति योजनाएँ
text: सुकमा जिला प्रशासन के आदिवासी कल्याण पृष्ठ पर छात्रावासों और आश्रमों की स्वीकृत संख्या तथा सीटों का विवरण दिया गया है। पृष्ठ की तालिका में विभिन्न श्रेणियों के लिए कुल 150 संस्थाएँ और 12,290 स्वीकृत सीटें बताई गई हैं; इसमें अनुसूचित जनजाति छात्रावास, प्राथमिक और माध्यमिक आश्रम, पिछड़ा वर्ग छात्रावास, कन्या शिक्षा परिसर और एकलव्य आदर्श आवासीय विद्यालय शामिल हैं। पृष्ठ पर छात्रवृत्ति, भोजन सहायता, पोस्ट-मैट्रिक छात्रवृत्ति और विशेष कोचिंग जैसी योजनाओं का भी वर्णन है। ये संख्याएँ पृष्ठ पर उपलब्ध प्रशासनिक स्नैपशॉट हैं; पृष्ठ पर स्पष्ट अद्यतन तिथि नहीं दिखती और तालिका के कुछ कॉलम/पंक्तियों का OCR या स्वरूपण अस्पष्ट है। वर्तमान पात्रता, राशि और सीट उपलब्धता के लिए नवीनतम विभागीय आदेश की पुष्टि आवश्यक है।

title: Tribal Welfare: Residential Institutions and Scholarships in Sukma
text: The official district Tribal Welfare page lists residential institutions and approved seats across several categories, including pre-matric and post-matric Scheduled Tribe hostels, primary and middle-level ashrams, a Backward Class post-matric hostel, a girls’ education complex, Eklavya Model Residential Schools and non-government ashram schools. Its table gives a stated total of 150 institutions and 12,290 approved seats, but the layout of some rows is ambiguous and the page does not show a clear last-updated date. The page also describes scholarship support, food assistance for post-matric hostel students, post-matric scholarships, minority scholarships and special coaching for students in classes 8, 10 and 12. Amounts and eligibility rules on the page may be dated; users should confirm them with the current department notification before relying on them.

title: सुकमा जिला परिचय पुस्तिका (2017): प्रशासनिक और सार्वजनिक सेवाओं का ऐतिहासिक स्नैपशॉट
text: सुकमा जिला प्रशासन की 12 जुलाई 2017 की “A brief introduction to District Sukma” पुस्तिका छह पृष्ठों की हिंदी PDF है। उपलब्ध PDF टेक्स्ट में 2011 जनगणना-आधारित स्थानीय निकाय/क्षेत्रवार जनसंख्या तालिकाएँ, तीन तहसीलों (कोंटा, सुकमा और छिंदगढ़) का प्रशासनिक संदर्भ, शिक्षा और स्वास्थ्य संस्थानों की तालिकाएँ, वन परिक्षेत्र, सिंचाई परियोजनाएँ, आंगनवाड़ी/महिला एवं बाल विकास, बाजार और राजस्व ग्रामों की जानकारी शामिल है। PDF का टेक्स्ट पुराने हिंदी फॉन्ट/OCR के कारण आंशिक रूप से विकृत है; इसलिए इस रिकॉर्ड में केवल विषय-सूची और ऐतिहासिक संदर्भ सुरक्षित किया गया है, न कि अस्पष्ट तालिकाओं के संख्यात्मक मान। इसे वर्तमान प्रशासनिक संरचना या वर्तमान सेवा उपलब्धता का प्रमाण न माना जाए।

title: Sukma District Department Pages: Content Coverage and Retrieval Limits
text: The official Sukma portal has dedicated pages for Mining, Revenue, and Women and Child Development, but the current English pages opened during collection contain little or no substantive explanatory text beyond the department heading, site navigation, and ownership information. The Mining page was last updated on 18 June 2020, the Revenue page on 20 January 2026, and the Women and Child Development page on 2 September 2026. These pages are useful as official source endpoints but should not be indexed as if they explain schemes, procedures, or current services. For WCD scheme details, individual dated notices may provide specific information; those notices must be indexed with their own dates and should not be generalized into current policy without checking status.

title: District profile and area discrepancy
text: The official Surajpur homepage reports area 4,996.26 km², population 789,043, literacy 60.95%, 547 villages and six blocks. The About District page instead says area 2,786.76 km² while repeating population 789,043. Treat area as disputed; do not collapse the two values without checking official district notifications and the source's intended boundary.
quality_flag: Official homepage and About page disagree on area.

title: Census 2011 population
text: The official demography page reports Census 2011 population 789,043: 398,381 males and 390,662 females. It also reports population density 283 persons per km². These are historical Census figures and should be kept separate from current estimates or later administrative changes.
quality_flag: Census-era data; density should be reconciled with area discrepancy.

title: Literacy and sex ratio
text: The official demography page reports literacy of 60.95% and a sex ratio of 980 females per 1,000 males. The source gives Census 2011 context. Verify the values against the Primary Census Abstract before treating them as canonical statistics.
quality_flag: Historical Census indicators; cross-check against PCA.

title: Scheduled Tribe and Scheduled Caste population
text: The official demography table lists 359,672 Scheduled Tribe residents and 42,830 Scheduled Caste residents. These values are presented in the page's Census 2011 table. Keep category labels and reference year intact; verify against the official Census PCA spreadsheet.
quality_flag: Census table values need spreadsheet cross-check.

title: Age 0–6 population
text: The official demography table lists 127,458 residents aged 0–6, comprising 65,088 males and 62,370 females. This is a Census 2011 indicator. Preserve the age band and census year to prevent confusion with current child-population estimates.
quality_flag: Historical Census figure; PCA verification pending.

title: Workers and occupational profile
text: The official demography page lists 380,851 total workers, including 191,826 main workers and 189,025 marginal workers. It further breaks out cultivators, agricultural labourers, household-industry workers and other workers. These figures are Census 2011-era labour categories, not current employment statistics.
quality_flag: Historical worker classifications; extract full table for canonical use.

title: District formation and history
text: The official About District page describes Surajpur as the 26th district of Chhattisgarh, carved out of the former Surguja district. It identifies Surajpur town as the administrative headquarters and gives the town's approximate coordinates. The page's narrative should be cross-checked against the original district-creation notification for exact legal dates.
quality_flag: Exact notification/date not extracted.

title: Historical place-name variants
text: The official About District page says Surajpur was earlier known as Daandbulla, later Suryapur, and now Surajpur. Treat these as names reported by the district portal; historical spellings and chronology need confirmation from gazetteers or archival sources.
quality_flag: Historical etymology not independently verified.

title: Languages
text: The official Surajpur homepage lists Hindi and Chhattisgarhi as languages. This is a qualitative language list, not a language-wise population table. Use Census mother-tongue data for quantitative language distributions and preserve local-language spellings in any multilingual records.
quality_flag: No language percentages provided.

title: Kudargarh and Mahamaya Mandir
text: The official tourism page lists Kudargarh and Mahamaya Mandir among major tourist attractions. This entry supports place discovery only; it does not verify festival dates, opening hours, visitor rules, temple history or current road conditions.
quality_flag: Tourism overview only; visitor logistics not extracted.

title: Dugdugi Stone and Shivpur Shiva Temple
text: The official Surajpur tourism page lists Dugdugi Stone, Hanuman Temple and Shivpur Shiva Temple among major attractions. Detailed archaeological descriptions, coordinates, conservation status and visitor facilities were not extracted in this record.
quality_flag: Attraction list only; historical detail not extracted.

title: Sarashor Temple and Kumeli Waterfall
text: The official homepage features Sarashor Temple and Lake and Kumeli Waterfall at Ramanujnagar. The images establish that the portal promotes these places, but they do not provide reliable details on access, seasonality, safety or facilities.
quality_flag: Image/gallery source; visitor details not verified.

title: District Survey Report 2025 revised
text: The official Mining page lists a District Survey Report dated 8 December 2025 and a revised Surajpur District Survey Report dated 23 January 2026. title: Surguja district overview
text: The official Surguja district portal identifies Ambikapur as district headquarters and describes Surguja as a district in northern Chhattisgarh. The state Tourism Board gives an area of about 5,732 km², but present-day boundary definitions and administrative changes should be checked before using this figure in a current profile.
quality_flag: Area value from Tourism Board; current portal overview does not show a matching headline table.

title: District history and princely state
text: The official Surguja About District page describes the region's earlier political history, including Rakshal-clan rule and Maharaja Amar Singh's coronation in 1826. The state Tourism Board provides a broader chronology, including Maratha and British periods. Treat these as summaries; detailed dates and contested claims should be checked against gazetteers and archival records.
quality_flag: Historical narratives require archival corroboration.

title: Census 2011 District Census Handbook Part A
text: The Census of India catalogue lists the Surguja District Census Handbook Part XII A, published in 2014. Part A contains the Village and Town Directory and information about local amenities such as schools, medical facilities, drinking water, transport, communications, electricity and banking. PDF and spreadsheets are listed but not extracted into this record.

text: The Chhattisgarh Tourism Board describes Surguja as part of the Surgujia dialectal region and says Surgujia is spoken there. Do not infer speaker percentages from these narratives; use Census mother-tongue data for quantitative language distribution.

title: Mainpat and pat landforms
text: The Tourism Board describes Surguja's mountainous landscape and distinctive highland tablelands called 'pat' formations, including Mainpat, Jarang Pat, Jonka Pat, Jamira Pat and Lahsun Pat. This is a useful geographic description; elevation, geology and land-cover figures need specialist sources.

text: The official Raipur district demography page describes the climate as tropical wet and dry. It says temperatures remain moderate for much of the year, while March through June can be extremely hot and April–May temperatures sometimes exceed 46°C. This is a qualitative summary from the district portal, not a live weather forecast or a climate-normal dataset.

title: Chhattisgarh cultural heritage overview
text:
IGNCA’s Chhattisgarh section links material on history, folklore, folk music and dance, instruments, proverbs, tribal communities, festivals, marriage customs, stories, literature, ornaments, tattooing, games, food, and cultural activities.
छत्तीसगढ़
quality_flag: overview; individual topic pages should be checked for completeness

title: Folk songs and folk dances of Chhattisgarh
text:
IGNCA describes folk song as an important part of Chhattisgarhi cultural life and names traditions including Sua, Dadariya, Karma, Danda, Phag, Chanouni, Bans geet, Raut geet and Panthi geet. It notes that some song traditions are performed with dance.
छत्तीसगढ़ के लोकगीत और लोकनृत्य
quality_flag: historical IGNCA page; review spellings and contemporary usage

title: Bhojli songs and tradition
text:
The page describes Bhojli as a seasonal women’s singing tradition associated with the month of Sawan, sowing grains in a basket, reverence for Bhojli Devi and nature, and carrying the grown plants to a water body after Raksha Bandhan. It also describes Bhojli as a symbol of friendship in some local practices.
भोजली
quality_flag: ritual details may vary by locality

title: Pandavani performance tradition
text:
IGNCA presents Pandavani as a narrative performance tradition based on the Pandava story from the Mahabharata. The article discusses Pardhan and Dewar performance lineages, the use of a tambura as a storytelling prop, audience-response singing, and the Kapalik and Vedamati styles; it notes Teejan Bai’s role in popularizing the form.
पंडवानी
quality_flag: historical ethnographic account; community labels and interpretations need careful context

title: Jas Geet devotional songs
text:
The page describes Jas Geet as devotional songs praising and petitioning the Goddess, especially associated with Navratri and Jawara practices. It discusses regional folk deities Dhanaiya and Koda(i)ya in the song tradition and their associations with crops in the account.
जस गीत
quality_flag: local devotional beliefs; present as tradition-specific descriptions

title: Bharthari folk ballad
text:
IGNCA discusses the Bharthari narrative involving King Bharthari and Gopichand, its links with Nath-panthi yogi traditions, and its adaptation into Chhattisgarhi performance. It describes solo singing with khanjari and later accompaniment by instruments such as tabla, harmonium, manjira and banjo.
भरथरी - लोकगाथा

title: Mythological references to Chhattisgarh
text:
IGNCA’s article records regional mythological traditions linking the area with Kosal, the story of Kaushalya and Rama, sages and ashrams, Dandakaranya, and sacred geography. These are cultural narratives and should be labeled as traditions or textual interpretations rather than verified historical facts.
छत्तीसगढ़ का पौराणिक संदर्भ
quality_flag: mythological/traditional account; do not present as established history

title: Historical references to Chhattisgarh
text:
IGNCA’s historical overview discusses Sirpur/Shripur, South Kosala, Buddhist associations, inscriptions and dynasties including Mauryas, Satavahanas, Guptas, Kalachuris and others. Some claims in this older overview are interpretive and should be checked against archaeological or scholarly sources.
छत्तीसगढ़ का ऐतिहासिक संदर्भ
quality_flag: historical claims need corroboration

title: Contribution to the freedom struggle
text:

text:

Cultural Archive

text:

नाचा

title: Traditional marriage customs in Chhattisgarh
text:
IGNCA’s interview-based page documents a sequence of marriage-related customs described by a cultural informant, including preparation of the wedding hearth, turmeric-and-oil rituals, ceremonial food, bathing and dressing the couple, welcoming the wedding party, circumambulation, and farewell songs. Practices can vary by community and locality; treat the page as one historical documentation rather than a universal description.
छत्तीसगढ़ के विवाह संस्कार

title: Mangrohan in Chhattisgarhi wedding traditions
text:
The IGNCA page describes Mangrohan as a ritual wooden figure or auspicious wooden symbol placed at a wedding mandap. The account associates it with witnessing and protecting the ceremony and records a local narrative connecting the custom with the Mahabharata story of Gandhari. Distinguish the documented local interpretation from independently established historical fact.
मंगरोहन
quality_flag: ritual interpretation and oral narrative; verify with community sources

title: Rikhi Kshatriya and regional folk instruments
text:
IGNCA profiles folk-instrument collector and performer Rikhi Kshatriya and describes a collection assembled from different regions and communities of Chhattisgarh. The page names instruments associated with places including Raipur, Rajnandgaon, Durg, Dantewada, Kanker, Surguja, Jashpur, Bilaspur and Bastar. It is useful as a source map for instrument names and regional associations, but the archive’s district references reflect its historical context and should be checked before modern geographic use.
रिखी क्षत्रिय और छत्तीसगढ़ के वाद्य
quality_flag: historical source; regional names and spellings need normalization

title: Folk instruments used in dance and ritual contexts
text:
The IGNCA instrument profile connects instruments with performance contexts such as Karma dance, devotional singing, Holi songs, weddings, community festivals and ritual observances. Examples named on the page include mandar, mridang, nagara, timki, tuddubudi and other locally named instruments. Use these as retrieval keywords and source pointers, not as an exhaustive or standardized instrument catalogue.
छत्तीसगढ़ के लोक वाद्य
quality_flag: spellings and instrument functions may vary by community; seek audio/field validation

title: Traditional ornaments documented in Chhattisgarh
text:
IGNCA’s illustrated archive page lists ornaments by body location and, in some cases, material. Examples include anklets and other foot ornaments, toe rings, bangles or bracelets, ear ornaments, nose ornaments, necklaces and waist ornaments. The source is valuable for collecting regional terminology and image references; some OCR and display text is corrupted, so individual names and materials should be verified against the page images or knowledgeable speakers.
छत्तीसगढ़ के आभूषण
quality_flag: image-heavy page; OCR errors; verify native spellings and materials

title: Godna or Gudna body tattooing
text:
The IGNCA index includes a dedicated page on Godna/Gudna, traditional tattooing. The topic can support questions about body art, cultural identity, motifs and intergenerational practice, but specific meanings should not be generalized across all communities without corroboration. This record is a source pointer and topic summary; the linked page’s detailed claims and image captions should be checked before adding finer-grained facts.
गोदना या गुदना
quality_flag: source pointer; detailed motif meanings need page-level and community validation

title: Traditional games of Chhattisgarh
text:
IGNCA provides a dedicated illustrated page about selected traditional games associated with Chhattisgarh. It can be used as an entry point for building a glossary of local game names, equipment, rules and occasions of play. Because game names and rules can differ between localities, extract each game separately and seek corroboration rather than treating the page as a complete statewide inventory.

title: Traditional foods and dishes
text:
The IGNCA index links to a page about selected Chhattisgarhi foods. This is a useful source pointer for a cuisine module covering dish names, ingredients, preparation methods, seasonal use and festival associations. The current record does not assert a complete dish list; individual dishes should be extracted from the source and validated with regional or community sources before being used as definitive answers.
छत्तीसगढ़ के कुछ स्वादिष्ट पकवान

title: Chhattisgarhi literary periods
text:
The IGNCA literature section organizes its overview into broad periods labelled Gatha Yug, the medieval Bhakti period, and the modern period. This structure can serve as a preliminary navigation taxonomy for literature-related questions, but period boundaries and author-level details should be corroborated with literary histories and primary bibliographic sources.

title: Chhattisgarh cultural activities and documentation
text:
The IGNCA index links a broader cultural-activities page and related profiles, including material titled Rupantar, a contribution by Padmavati Devi, and a contribution by Margaret Das. These entries are potential leads for documenting practitioners, researchers and cultural initiatives. Individual pages should be reviewed before assigning a specific contribution, community, date or location.
छत्तीसगढ़ की संस्कृति और उससे जुड़ी हुई गतिविधियाँ

title: Tribal communities in the IGNCA Chhattisgarh archive
text:
The IGNCA archive has a dedicated page on tribal communities and a linked page on the Gond community. These historical pages can help identify community names and topics such as oral traditions, festivals, livelihood, music and customary practices. They should not be treated as current demographic data or as uniform descriptions of any community; terminology and claims need review with contemporary, community-led sources.

text:

Modern spellings, subgroup terminology and historical claims should be checked against reliable contemporary and community-authored sources.

title: Folk music and dance topic index
text:

text:

title: Source quality and reuse notes for the IGNCA Chhattisgarh archive
text:
The Chhattisgarh pages in the IGNCA COIL-Net collection are an older cultural archive, with copyright notices on individual pages. For RAG use, store the source title and URL, retrieval date, content type, summary, uncertainty and reuse status. Historical spellings, district boundaries, demographic descriptions and OCR from illustrated pages should be verified; full poems, songs, proverbs and folk tales should not be bulk-republished without permission or a clear licence.

title: Dondi-Poha: a circle-and-call traditional game
text:
IGNCA's account describes Dondi-Poha as a group game played around a circle drawn on the ground. One player stands outside and calls a rhythmic sequence while the players inside respond; a name may then be called as part of the play. The page presents it through an interview with Dr. Satyabhama Adil. This is a source-specific description and should be checked with local players for current rules and dialect wording.
डोन्डी-पोहा
quality_flag: rules and wording may vary; no full call-and-response lyrics reproduced

title: Bhounda: spinning-top play
text:
IGNCA identifies Bhounda as a popular game involving spinning a top, accompanied by a short rhythmic chant. The archive links play and spoken or sung rhythm, showing that traditional games can include oral-performance elements as well as physical rules. The record intentionally summarizes the chant instead of reproducing it at length.
भौंड़ा
quality_flag: source uses regional spelling; confirm the game's local name and variants

title: Khudua: a local name for a kabaddi-like game
text:
The IGNCA page says that a game called Khudua in the account is known as kabaddi elsewhere, and notes that a chant accompanies play. This is useful evidence for regional naming variation, but should not be interpreted as proof that all rules are identical to modern standardized kabaddi.
खुदुआ
quality_flag: distinguish local oral-game description from standardized sport rules

title: Regional ornament vocabulary: foot ornaments
text:
The IGNCA illustrated list includes several foot-ornament names, such as pairi, paijan, lachha, saanti and toe ornaments such as bichhiya/bichhua/chutki. The page associates some items with materials including silver or bronze. Because the original page contains imperfect text rendering, these names and material associations should be checked against the images and local speakers before being treated as standardized spellings.

title: Regional ornament vocabulary: ear and nose ornaments
text:
The IGNCA list names ear ornaments including tarki, chhumka, dhar, khinwa and karan phool, and nose ornaments including phulli and nath. These are source spellings from an older illustrated archive and may represent local or variant forms; confirm each term and its use with regional speakers and the page images.
कान और नाक के आभूषण

title: Regional ornament vocabulary: necklaces and waist ornaments
text:

title: Godna: tattoo motifs and community-specific meanings
text:
The IGNCA page describes Godna/Gudna as a body-art tradition and mentions motifs such as scorpion, peacock, sun, star, moon, lion, horse and other forms. It notes that motif design and significance differ across communities and that tattoos may appear on different parts of the body. These are historical-source claims; meanings should be attributed to the specific community or informant and not generalized statewide.
गोदना या गुदना

title: Godna: historical techniques and materials described in the archive
text:
The IGNCA page records historical descriptions of tattooing materials and techniques, including plant-derived preparations and thorn-based application, and discusses Baiga women's tattoo traditions. These descriptions should be treated as historical documentation, not as instructions for practice or as medical advice. Any present-day account should be confirmed with practitioners and community-led sources.

title: Regional folk-instrument names and locations in an older archive
text:
IGNCA's profile of collector Rikhi Kshatriya associates named instruments with historical regional locations: dafda and nisan with Raipur, ronjo with Rajnandgaon, dahank with Durg, tudbudi with Dantewada, hirnang with Kanker, singabaja with Surguja, tamariya with Jashpur, hirki and dhunguru with Bilaspur, and tamok with Bastar. Preserve these as archive-attributed associations, not definitive modern district boundaries or exhaustive provenance.

title: Madiya/Muria drum in community festival performance
text:
The IGNCA instrument profile describes a Madiya/Muria drum associated with Muria communities in the Bastar region. It notes a wooden body with animal-skin drumheads and describes its role in a community festival and night-time dancing. The source's terminology and festival description should be corroborated with current community-led documentation; the record summarizes rather than reproduces the full account.
माड़िया ढोल

title: Chulmati: preparing the wedding hearth
text:
In the IGNCA interview on marriage customs, Chulmati is described as women bringing soil from a village pond to make the hearth used for cooking during wedding preparations. This is one informant's description of a local custom, not a universal practice across all communities or present-day weddings.
चुलमाटि
quality_flag: interview-based account; local and community variation expected

title: Tel-chadhi and wedding preparations
text:
The IGNCA interview describes a turmeric mixed with oil ritual performed for bride and groom in their respective households, with relatives applying the mixture and community members invited. The record captures the source's summary of the ritual; details may differ by family, caste, tribe, region and contemporary practice.
तेल चढ़ी
quality_flag: interview-based account; do not universalize ritual sequence

title: Paradhani: welcoming the wedding party
text:
The IGNCA marriage interview identifies Paradhani as the welcoming of the arriving wedding party at the bride's home, accompanied in the account by women's songs. This provides a cultural term and its described context for a Chhattisgarhi glossary. Confirm local pronunciation, spelling and current usage with speakers from the relevant area.
परधनी
quality_flag: single interview; local pronunciation and practices may differ

title: IGNCA Chhattisgarh cultural archive: page-level reuse restriction
text:
The reviewed IGNCA pages for games, ornaments, Godna, wedding customs and folk instruments display copyright notices; some explicitly prohibit reprinting without written permission. For this dataset, store attributed summaries, source links and review notes. Do not distribute large verbatim extracts, full song texts or story texts unless permission or a suitable licence is confirmed.
IGNCA स्रोत एवं पुनःउपयोग सीमा

title: Pola festival and agricultural life
text:
IGNCA describes Pola as a festival connected with farming and the agricultural cycle, observed around the new moon in the Bhadrapada period. The page documents worship of livestock, decorated bullocks, clay bull toys for children, household offerings and special foods. It also records local games and bullock-cart competitions. Treat the timing and practices as the archive's account; current observance varies by locality.
पोला
quality_flag: historical source; confirm present-day practices and local festival dates

title: Pola and clay bull toys
text:
The IGNCA Pola entry describes children receiving or worshipping clay bull figures and carrying them from house to house, where they may receive small gifts or offerings. This detail connects the festival with children's play, craft objects and the symbolic importance of cattle in agrarian life. Do not assume every village follows the same custom.
पोला में मिट्टी के बैल
quality_flag: community practices may vary; summary only

title: Hartalika Teej in the IGNCA festival account
text:
The IGNCA festival interview describes Hartalika Teej as observed on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada. It records fasting, worship of Shiva and Parvati, offerings and an overnight ritual in the source's local account. The page also explains the custom of married daughters returning to their parental homes for Teej. These are attributed cultural descriptions, not a universal account of all observances.
हरतालिका तीज
quality_flag: ritual practices and fasting vary; avoid prescribing religious practice

title: Pola and Teej as a linked seasonal-social sequence
text:
The IGNCA account places Teej soon after Pola and links the festival period with married women and daughters travelling to their parental homes. This can support questions about the social calendar of festivals, family visits and seasonal customs in the source's documented setting. Exact dates depend on the lunar calendar, and the description should not be generalized to every household.
पोला और तीजा
quality_flag: source-specific social custom; verify contemporary and community variation

title: Month-by-month agricultural activity calendar
text:
The IGNCA page reproduces a month-wise agricultural activity overview attributed to Indira Gandhi Agricultural University. It includes seasonal field preparation, sowing, transplanting, weeding, irrigation, harvesting, storage and horticultural tasks. The calendar is useful as a historical reference for agriculture-related retrieval, but it should not be used as current agronomic advice without checking updated agricultural university or extension guidance.
प्रमुख कृषि कार्य
quality_flag: legacy calendar; not current farming advice; modern crop timing and districts may differ

title: Rice cultivation and the monsoon season
text:
In its month-wise calendar, the IGNCA page highlights rice transplanting and monsoon-season field management in June and July, including bunding, transplanting and weeding. It also notes the need to manage excess rainfall and maintain moisture. This is a high-level historical description; crop recommendations should be checked against current regional advisories.
धान की खेती और वर्षा ऋतु
quality_flag: historical agricultural description; verify with current extension sources

title: Agricultural proverbs as traditional knowledge
text:
The IGNCA page collects agricultural sayings and explains them in relation to sowing time, ploughing, crop care and irrigation. It also describes three broad agro-climatic regions using an older district framework. For RAG, store proverb themes and concise interpretations, not bulk verbatim sayings; update the geographic classification using current agricultural sources before using it for location-specific answers.
कृषि की लोकोक्तियाँ
quality_flag: copyright notice; old district boundaries and agro-climatic figures need verification

title: Rajim as an archaeological site
text:
The IGNCA article describes inscriptions, coins and pottery finds associated with Rajim and discusses evidence used to study different historical periods in the area. It mentions an inscription associated with the Rajiv Lochan temple and historical rulers. These are claims reported by the archive; inscription dates, readings and historical interpretations should be cross-checked with archaeological publications before being presented as settled facts.
राजिम का पुरातात्विक महत्व

title: Rajiv Lochan temple architecture and iconography
text:
IGNCA describes the Rajiv Lochan temple at Rajim as a Vishnu temple with a four-armed black-stone image and architectural elements including a mandapa supported by stone pillars. The page also notes sculptural imagery and subsidiary shrines in the temple complex. The archive associates the temple with an inscription of the Nala ruler Vilasatunga and an eighth-century date; confirm dating and architectural details with current archaeological or heritage sources.
राजीव लोचन का मन्दिर

title: Rajim's river confluence and religious landscape
text:
The IGNCA temple entry describes Rajim as a confluence area associated with the Mahanadi, Pairi and Sondur rivers, with temples and pilgrimage practices around the river landscape. This record supports retrieval about the relationship between geography, sacred sites and ritual practice. River names, exact confluence geography and current pilgrimage details should be checked against authoritative maps and contemporary sources.

title: Jas Geet devotional song tradition

title: History of Bastar District
text: The official Bastar district history page states that Jagdalpur is the headquarters of Bastar district and Bastar division. It describes the region as historically associated with Dakshin Kaushal and says the Bastar princely state was established around 1324 CE by Anaam Dev, who left Warangal and established a kingdom in Bastar. The page names rulers including Hamir Dev, Baital Dev, Purushottam Dev, Pratap Dev, Dikpal Dev and Rajpal Dev. It says the initial capital was Bastar town and was later moved to Jagdalpur. Maharaja Praveer Chandra Bhanj Dev is described as the last ruler, with the period 1936–1948, and the princely state is said to have merged with India in 1948. The page also notes that Kanker and Dantewada were carved out in 1999, and lists Bastar Mahal, Bastar Dussehra, Dalpat Sagar, Chitrakote and Tirathgarh waterfalls, and Kutumsar and Kailash caves as tourist attractions. The page reports Census 2011 population of 834,375 (413,706 men and 420,669 women) and mentions Gond, Maria, Muria, Bhatra, Halba and Dhruva communities. Historical and population details are reported as stated by the district website; population and administrative figures should be interpreted with their reference dates.

title: बस्तर जिले का इतिहास
text: बस्तर जिला प्रशासन की आधिकारिक हिंदी वेबसाइट के अनुसार, बस्तर जिले और बस्तर संभाग का मुख्यालय जगदलपुर है। वेबसाइट क्षेत्र को ऐतिहासिक रूप से दक्षिण कौशल से जोड़ती है और बताती है कि लगभग 1324 ईस्वी में अन्नम देव ने वारंगल छोड़कर बस्तर में रियासत स्थापित की। वेबसाइट में हमीर देव, बैताल देव, पुरुषोत्तम देव, प्रताप देव, दिकपाल देव और राजपाल देव जैसे शासकों का उल्लेख है। प्रारंभिक राजधानी बस्तर में थी, जिसे बाद में जगदलपुर स्थानांतरित किया गया। वेबसाइट महाराजा प्रवीर चन्द्र भंज देव को अंतिम शासक बताती है और रियासत का भारत में विलय 1948 में बताती है। पृष्ठ में 1999 में कांकेर और दंतेवाड़ा को अलग जिले बनाए जाने का भी उल्लेख है। बस्तर महल, बस्तर दशहरा, दलपत सागर, चित्रकोट और तीरथगढ़ जलप्रपात तथा कुटुमसर और कैलाश गुफाओं को पर्यटन स्थलों में गिना गया है। वेबसाइट 2011 की जनगणना के अनुसार जनसंख्या 8,34,375 बताती है। इन ऐतिहासिक और जनसांख्यिकीय विवरणों को वेबसाइट-आधारित जानकारी के रूप में रखें और आंकड़ों के संदर्भ वर्ष को सुरक्षित रखें।
category: जिला इतिहास; रियासत; जनजातीय संस्कृति; पर्यटन

title: Bastar District Demography — Census 2011
text: The official Bastar district demography page presents population statistics based on Census 2011. It reports a total population of 834,375, consisting of 413,706 males and 420,669 females. These figures describe the district as represented on the page and relate to Census 2011; they should not be presented as current population estimates.

text: बस्तर जिला प्रशासन की आधिकारिक हिंदी वेबसाइट के अनुसार, जिला छत्तीसगढ़ के बस्तर संभाग के अंतर्गत आता है। जिला कलेक्टर एवं दंडाधिकारी जिले के प्रशासक होते हैं और कानून-व्यवस्था बनाए रखने, नियमों के पालन तथा सरकारी योजनाओं के क्रियान्वयन के लिए जिम्मेदार होते हैं। यह पृष्ठ प्रशासनिक भूमिका का वर्णन करता है; इसे सभी प्रशासनिक इकाइयों की संपूर्ण सूची नहीं माना जाना चाहिए।

title: Economy of Bastar District
text: The official Bastar district economy page identifies agriculture and collection of forest produce as major foundations of the district economy. Paddy is described as the main crop, especially during the kharif season. Other crops mentioned include urad, arhar, jowar, maize, sesame, linseed, mustard, gram, wheat and kodo-kutki. The page says that collecting and selling forest produce supplements agricultural income. Items listed include tendu leaves, lac, tamarind, amchur and other forest products. Animal husbandry, poultry and fisheries also support livelihoods. The page discusses low irrigation and fertilizer use and suggests rainwater harvesting as a possibility. Some wording on the page appears to be machine-translated or unclear, so exact technical figures should be verified before reuse.
category: Local economy; agriculture; forest produce; livelihoods

title: बस्तर जिले की अर्थव्यवस्था
text: बस्तर जिला प्रशासन की आधिकारिक वेबसाइट के अनुसार, जिले की अर्थव्यवस्था का प्रमुख आधार कृषि और वनोपज का संग्रहण है। खरीफ मौसम में धान मुख्य फसल है। वेबसाइट में उड़द, अरहर, ज्वार, मक्का, तिल, अलसी, सरसों, चना, गेहूं और कोदो-कुटकी जैसी अन्य फसलों का भी उल्लेख है। वनोपज का संग्रह और बिक्री कृषि से होने वाली आय को सहारा देते हैं। वेबसाइट में तेंदूपत्ता, लाख, इमली, आमचूर और अन्य वन उत्पादों का उल्लेख है। पशुपालन, मुर्गीपालन और मत्स्य पालन भी आजीविका में योगदान देते हैं। पृष्ठ सिंचाई और उर्वरक के कम उपयोग पर चर्चा करता है तथा वर्षा जल संचयन की संभावना बताता है। पृष्ठ की कुछ भाषा अस्पष्ट या मशीन-अनुवाद जैसी है, इसलिए सटीक तकनीकी आंकड़ों को उपयोग से पहले सत्यापित करें।

title: Bastar District Survey Report 2026 — overview and geography
text: The District Survey Report (DSR) for Bastar district was compiled by the Regional Office of the Directorate of Geology and Mining, Jagdalpur, using information provided by different departments through the District Mining Officer, Bastar. The report cover identifies it as a 2026 report for sand mining or riverbed mining. Its introduction places Bastar in southeastern Chhattisgarh and identifies Jagdalpur as district headquarters. The report lists seven blocks: Jagdalpur, Bastar, Bakawand, Darbha, Tokapal, Bastanar and Lohandiguda. It cites Census 2011 population of 834,375 (413,706 males and 420,669 females) and says more than 70% of the population belongs to indigenous tribal communities. The report gives geographical area as 6,596.90 km². These demographic figures are historical 2011 Census data, not current estimates.

title: Bastar District Survey Report 2026 — overview of mining activities

It reports six operational or allotted limestone mines and names locations including Tokapal, Rajur, Badanji, Mongarapal and Bastar. The report also mentions 107 stone quarries. For minor minerals and riverbed materials, it describes sand and clay as construction inputs and says two sand blocks have been leased along the Bhaskali River near Bajawand village. These counts and locations reflect the report's stated snapshot and should be checked against later mining department updates.
